extracted.intended_audience: British and American abolitionist audiences, churchmen, and the general public
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted from Frederick Douglass's public lectures and a public letter; rhetorical and evidentiary criteria he uses to describe and condemn slavery and to persuade British and American audiences. Focus is on moral, legal, social, and rhetorical facets of abolitionist argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's legal property relation to slave
rubrics_metrics.description: A master 'claims and exercises a right of property in the person of a fellow-man' and the law gives the master absolute power over the slave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: the master may 'work him, flog him, hire him out, sell him, and, in certain contingencies, kill him, with perfect impunity.' The slave is treated as a 'chattel' in law, having 'no wife, no children, no country, and no home.' This legal status is presented as a primary basis for condemning slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical cruelties and instruments of domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery is enforced through physical instruments and brutal practices that ensure obedience and destroy manhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated instruments and methods: 'the whip, the chain, the gag, the thumb-screw, the pillory, the bowie knife the pistol, and the blood-hound.' These are described as 'necessary and unvarying accompaniments of the system' and used to 'imbrute and destroy' the slave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery's mutilation of moral, intellectual, and religious nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond physical abuse, slavery 'mar[s] and deface[s]' the slave's moral, intellectual, and religious faculties, blunting conscience and severing the slave from God and moral responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass argues 'the first business of the enslaver of men [is] to blunt, deaden, and destroy the central principle of human responsibility.' The loss of conscience is framed as catastrophic both for the individual and for social trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and social prohibition of education
rubrics_metrics.description: Most slave states have laws 'absolutely prohibitory of education among the slaves'; teaching a slave to read is criminalized (fines, imprisonment, sometimes death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass gives the common rationale: slaveholders view education as 'utterly subversive of the slave system.' He uses his own experience—master's reaction when told Douglass could read—to illustrate that literacy threatens the system by making slaves discontent and capable of escape and resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic exploitation and denial of fruits of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Slaves toil so that others live in ease; they cannot own or enjoy the results of their labor and are forbidden from appropriating what they produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'He toils that another may reap the fruit; he is industrious that another may live in idleness; he eats unbolted meal that another may eat the bread of fine flour.' Douglass emphasizes that taking the slave's earnings is treated as rightful by owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family separation and denial of domestic rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery routinely separates families; in law the slave has 'no wife, no children,' and relatives can be sold, torn from each other, and reduced to property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass recounts personal wounds (sisters and brother in bondage, grandmother turned out to die) and frames family destruction as a central moral horror of slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of civil liberties (speech, press, assembly, petition, locomotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slaves lack basic civil liberties: they have no freedom of speech, press, assembly, petition, or free movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass contrasts the slave's condition with the Irish poor: though oppressed, the Irish can assemble, petition, and publish; the slave cannot. This absence of civic channels is presented as evidence of slavery's totalitarian nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silencing of the enslaved (absence of a voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A telling mark of slavery is that the enslaved are 'dumb'—there is no authentic voice from the enslaved to testify about their condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass writes that if one were to ask a slave his feelings about enslavement, one would get silence; this 'dumbness' is used rhetorically to emphasize the moral urgency of speaking for the enslaved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of official laws and public records as proof of cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The slave codes and public advertisements in the slave states provide incontrovertible documentary evidence of the system's cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass refuses to rely solely on anecdote; he cites 'extracts from the slave codes' and runaway advertisements describing branding, chains, and scars to prove that the law itself authorizes cruel treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypocrisy of religion and complicity of clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: Slaveholding is sanctioned by a corrupted religion and the complicity of churchmen and clergy, making the American church morally culpable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass promises to 'make use of you as a means of exposing the character of the American church and clergy' and urges English ministers to embrace the cause; the charge is that religion is being used to justify brutality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirth under bondage is not evidence of contentment
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable singing or dancing by slaves does not prove happiness; such mirth can coexist with brutal subjugation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass explains that occasional joy 'only proves ... that though slavery is armed with a thousand stings, it is not able entirely to kill the elastic spirit of the bondman.' His point is an anti-pattern: do not mistake outward signs for genuine welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery undermines national peace and moral order
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation that enslaves millions cannot achieve a sound and lasting peace; slavery corrupts national justice and provokes agitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass argues that measures intended to secure quiet have produced alarm and war, and that 'while this nation is guilty of the enslavement of three millions ... it is as idle to think of having a sound and lasting peace.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Education breeds liberation and is therefore suppressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning to read and write opens 'the treasures of freedom' and thus is actively suppressed by slaveholders who fear it will produce discontent and escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass's personal anecdote: when his mistress discovered he could read, his master said 'I was ruined, and my value as a slave destroyed'—a concrete illustration of the system's logic for prohibiting education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for freedom over homeland despite hardships
rubrics_metrics.description: True love of personal freedom leads formerly enslaved people to prefer remaining free even under hardship rather than returning to slavery, undermining claims that slavery is benign because people are 'attached' to their birthplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass notes that many freed people would return to the South if emancipation occurred, but the reason they remain in the North is an 'intense love of personal freedom'—this rebuts simplistic assumptions about loyalty to place being equivalent to contentment under slavery.
